scenario_provenance.archetype_label: Multi-focus on Practices 3 & 4 (analyze data; interpret results)
validity_rules: OBSERVATIONAL comparison only (no random assignment -> no causal claim)
means differ but spreads overlap so an over-strong claim is refutable

sources.note: the item stem's verb must match the scored demand

prompt: In an observational garden study, plants in sunny spots had a mean recorded height of 51 cm (SD about 12) and plants in shaded spots had a mean of 45 cm (SD about 12). A student claims: "plants in sunny spots always have a higher recorded height than plants in shaded spots." Which statement best justifies whether the data support this claim?

options.text: These results prove that plants in sunny spots will always outperform plants in shaded spots on recorded height in any future study or population.

misconception_source.label: Over-generalized beyond the data using definitive language

sources.note: 2025 CR Report: conclusions must use non-definitive language ('convincing evidence'), never 'proves'/'always'; and must not generalize beyond the studied population

options.text: Since the mean for plants in sunny spots (51) is greater than for plants in shaded spots (45), every member of plants in sunny spots must have a higher recorded height than every member of plants in shaded spots.

misconception_source.label: Treated a difference in means as a claim about every individual value

sources.note: on-average differences must not be over-read as claims about all individual values; overlap matters

options.text: The claim is correct because plants in sunny spots clearly did better on recorded height.

misconception_source.label: Restated the claim without citing statistical evidence

sources.ref: AP_STATISTICS_2027_CED_FACT_PACK.md S4/S6 (skill 4.B; task verbs) + S10 'General exam-wide conventions'
sources.note: a justification must reference the statistical evidence, not merely restate the claim

options.text: On average plants in sunny spots had a higher recorded height (mean 51 vs 45), so the data support a typical difference; but because both SDs are about 12, the distributions overlap substantially, so the data do not support a claim that plants in sunny spots are always higher.

parts.prompt: In an observational garden study, plants in sunny spots had a mean recorded height of 51 cm (SD about 12) and plants in shaded spots had a mean of 45 cm (SD about 12). A student claims: "plants in sunny spots always have a higher recorded height than plants in shaded spots." Which statement best justifies whether the data support this claim?

criteria.description: Selects the justification that affirms the on-average difference while rejecting the over-strong 'always' claim due to overlap.

provenance.note: Authored conceptual frame; correctness from authored justification taxonomy.
